title: Names, errors and dates in practice
summary: Readable formulas with names and Tables, error handling, and date maths on the practice shift data.

lessons.title: Named ranges and structured references
lessons.body:
A **name** is a label for a cell, a range or a constant, so a formula reads like a sentence. Select the cell, type a name in the Name Box (left of the formula bar) and press Enter, or use Formulas > Define Name. A name starts with a letter or underscore, has no spaces (use `Bonus_Rate`), and cannot look like a cell address (`Q1` is rejected). Open the Name Manager with **Ctrl+F3** to edit, delete or see what each name points at.

If G1 holds the bonus per filled shift and is named `BonusRate`:

```text
=C2*BonusRate
```

A name always points at the same cell, so it behaves like an absolute reference without the dollar signs.

**Tables go further.** Load `shifts.csv` from the practice data, press Ctrl+T and call the table `tblShifts`. Its columns now have names you can use in any formula:

| Reference | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `tblShifts[status]` | every value in the status column |
| `[@status]` | the status on this row (inside the table) |
| `tblShifts[[#Headers],[status]]` | the header cell |
| `tblShifts[#Totals]` | the total row |

Share of shifts that were completed:

```text
=COUNTIFS(tblShifts[status],"completed")/ROWS(tblShifts[id])
```

That is 828 / 1019 = 81.3%. Emergency shifts that were cancelled:

```text
=COUNTIFS(tblShifts[status],"cancelled",tblShifts[is_emergency],1)
```

The answer is 33.

**Why this beats `$H$2:$H$1020`.**

- The reference grows when you paste more rows under the table, so formulas, pivots and charts stay correct.
- The formula can be read aloud, which makes review easier.
- You cannot end up with mismatched range sizes, a common cause of `#VALUE!` in SUMIFS.

**Limits.** A name that points at a plain range does not grow by itself. Deleting the cells a name points at turns it into `#REF!`. Keep names short and consistent (a prefix such as `tbl` for tables helps), and delete unused ones in Name Manager. A name can also be the source of a data validation list, which the validation lesson uses.
keyPoints: A name labels a cell, range or constant; Ctrl+F3 opens the Name Manager.
A Table column reference like tblShifts[status] grows with the data.
[@col] means this row's value inside a Table.
Names pointing at plain ranges do not grow and can break to #REF!.
lessons.interviewAngle: Tests rarely ask for named ranges by name, but readable formulas and Tables show care. Say: "I turn the export into a Table and use structured references so the formulas grow with the data." That is honest at a moderate level. Do not claim dynamic named ranges built with OFFSET unless you have practised them.

choices: It grows automatically when rows are added to the Table and reads clearly
It calculates faster on every workbook
It ignores blank rows that the fixed range would count
It works in every version of Excel including the web and Mac
exercises.explanation: A structured reference follows the Table as it grows and names the column. Speed and blank-row handling are not the reason.

exercises.prompt: Which keyboard shortcut opens the Name Manager?
exercises.explanation: Ctrl+F3 lists every name, its value and what it refers to.

exercises.prompt: With the practice shifts loaded as `tblShifts`, write one formula for the share of shifts that have a filled time, and state the figure you should get.
exercises.answer:
```text
=COUNTA(tblShifts[filled_at])/ROWS(tblShifts[id])
```
906 of 1019 shifts have a filled time, so the result is 88.9%. COUNTA counts non-empty cells; the 113 blanks are cancelled and open shifts that were never filled.
rubric: Uses structured references, not cell addresses
Counts non-empty filled_at values over all rows

lessons.title: Errors, IFERROR and silent wrong answers
lessons.body:
Excel errors are messages, and each points at a cause.

| Error | Usual cause | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `#DIV/0!` | dividing by zero or an empty cell | test the denominator first |
| `#N/A` | a lookup found nothing | check the key; label with `IFNA` |
| `#VALUE!` | text where a number is needed, such as a stray space | clean the data |
| `#REF!` | a deleted reference, or a VLOOKUP column number too large | repair the reference |
| `#NAME?` | a misspelt function or name, or text without quotes | check spelling; XLOOKUP in an old version |
| `#NUM!` | an impossible number | check inputs |
| `#SPILL!` | a dynamic array blocked by other cells | clear the cells in its path |
| `#####` | column too narrow, or a negative date | widen the column |

**IFERROR** replaces any error with a fallback: `=IFERROR(AVERAGEIFS(...),"No filled shifts")`. Use a clear label, not 0, because 0 hours to fill would read as an instant fill. Where only one error is expected use the narrower tool: `IFNA` for lookups, or `=IF(B2=0,"",C2/B2)` for ratios. `IFERROR` also hides mistakes of your own, such as a `#REF!`.

**The dangerous case is no error at all.** In `shifts.csv`, 113 shifts have no `filled_at` (93 cancelled and 20 open). A hours-to-fill column of `=([@filled_at]-[@requested_at])*24` treats the empty cell as 0, which is the year 1900. The answer is a negative number of about -1.1 million hours with no warning, and `IFERROR` would not catch it. Guard the blank:

```text
=IF([@filled_at]="","",([@filled_at]-[@requested_at])*24)
```

`AVERAGE` skips the empty text, so the column averages 9.52 hours over the 906 filled shifts. Without the guard the average is nonsense. Always scan a new column with MIN, MAX and COUNT before trusting it: a minimum below zero is the clue.

**Auditing tools** (Formulas tab): Error Checking, Trace Precedents and Dependents, Show Formulas, and **Evaluate Formula**, which steps through a formula one operation at a time. In the formula bar, select part of a formula and press F9 to see its value, then Esc to put it back.
keyPoints: Read the error: #DIV/0!, #N/A, #REF!, #NAME? and #SPILL! each point at a cause.
Use IFNA for lookups and an explicit test for ratios; IFERROR hides real mistakes.
Blank cells in date maths give wrong answers without any error: guard them.
lessons.interviewAngle: A common test question is a formula that "returns an error" or a column of strange numbers. Describe your habit: read the error, check inputs, then add a guard. Mention checking MIN, MAX and COUNT of new columns. This is moderate-level work you can claim from your real reporting and checking.

exercises.prompt: An AVERAGEIFS for one pharmacy returns #DIV/0! because it has no filled shifts. What is the best handling?
choices: Wrap it so it shows a label such as "No filled shifts"
Wrap it so it shows 0 hours
Delete the pharmacy's row from the report
exercises.explanation: A label tells the reader there is no data. 0 would look like an instant fill and silently mislead.

exercises.prompt: Which error appears when a VLOOKUP column number is larger than the number of columns in the table array?
exercises.explanation: The column index points outside the range, which Excel reports as #REF!.

exercises.prompt: A new column `=(C2-B2)*24` is meant to give hours to fill, but a few rows show about -1,100,000. Explain the cause and give the fixed formula.
exercises.answer: C2 (filled_at) is empty for cancelled and open shifts. Excel treats an empty cell as 0, so the formula subtracts a 2026 date from 1900 and returns a huge negative number with no error. Fix: `=IF(C2="","",(C2-B2)*24)`. Check afterwards that MIN is not negative and that the average is about 9.52 hours.
rubric: Identifies the empty filled_at as the cause
Explains an empty cell counts as 0
Gives an IF guard that returns an empty string

lessons.title: Dates, times and TEXT in practice
lessons.body:
Dates are numbers, so most date work is arithmetic plus a display format. Take shift 1001 from the practice data. B2 is requested 2026-01-03 05:23:10, C2 is filled 2026-01-03 22:03:41 and D2 is starts 2026-01-05 07:00:00.

| Formula | Result |
|---|---|
| `=(C2-B2)*24` | 16.68 hours to fill |
| `=(D2-B2)*24` | 49.61 hours of lead time |
| `=INT(B2)` (format as date) | 2026-01-03 |
| `=TEXT(B2,"yyyy-mm")` | 2026-01 |
| `=TEXT(B2,"ddd")` | Sat |
| `=WEEKDAY(B2,2)` | 6 (Monday is 1) |
| `=HOUR(B2)` | 5 |

**Is it really a date?** Excel often converts ISO text such as `2026-01-03 05:23:10` when it opens a CSV, but a file loaded another way may keep it as text. A real date is right-aligned, and switching the format to General shows a number such as 46025.22. For text, rebuild it: `=DATEVALUE(LEFT(A2,10))+TIMEVALUE(MID(A2,12,8))`.

**Counting by month.** Do not compare dates with a month name. Use a half-open interval, because times have decimals:

```text
=COUNTIFS(tblShifts[requested_at],">="&DATE(2026,3,1),
          tblShifts[requested_at],"<"&DATE(2026,4,1))
```

That returns 105, the shifts requested in March 2026. A test of `"<="&DATE(2026,3,31)` would drop everything after midnight on the 31st.

**TEXT** turns a number or date into formatted text: `="Filled in "&TEXT((C2-B2)*24,"0.0")&" hours"` gives "Filled in 16.7 hours". Common codes are `yyyy-mm-dd`, `mmm`, `ddd`, `0.0%` and `#,##0`. Two cautions. In a time format `mm` after `h` means minutes, otherwise months. And the result is **text**, so a pivot sorts "Apr" before "Jan"; for charts keep a real date and group by month in the pivot, or sort by `yyyy-mm`.

**Other tools.** `EOMONTH(date,0)` is month end, `NETWORKDAYS` counts weekdays, `WORKDAY(date,5)` moves forward five working days, and `DATEDIF(start,end,"m")` counts whole months and `"y"` whole years. Microsoft documents DATEDIF as a legacy function that can give wrong results, so use plain subtraction (`=end-start`) for days, keep DATEDIF for whole months or years, and avoid its `"md"` unit. `TODAY()` and `NOW()` recalculate on every open, so do not use them in a figure you want frozen.
keyPoints: Dates are day counts; multiply a difference by 24 for hours.
Check a date is real: right-aligned, and a number under General format.
Count a month with >= first day and < first day of next month.
TEXT returns text; keep real dates for charts and pivots.
lessons.interviewAngle: Time-to-fill and month labels come up in almost every operations test. Explain the days-to-hours conversion and the half-open date interval, which shows care. You reported time to fill in SQL, so you can say you know the metric and are showing the Excel version.

exercises.prompt: Which formula counts shifts requested in March 2026 when `requested_at` includes times?
exercises.explanation: A start-inclusive, end-exclusive interval catches every time of day in March. The 31 March version stops at midnight and also includes earlier months.

exercises.prompt: A time difference is 0.5 days. How many hours is that? (Number only.)
Shift 1002 was requested 2025-12-27 22:55:55 and filled 2025-12-28 12:05:40. Show the formula for hours to fill and roughly what it returns, then say how you would label each shift by request month.
exercises.answer: Hours to fill: `=(C2-B2)*24`, which is about 13.16 hours (13 hours 9 minutes 45 seconds). Month label: `=TEXT(B2,"yyyy-mm")`, giving 2025-12 for this shift. For a pivot, keep the real date and group by Months and Years instead, because TEXT results are text.
rubric: Subtracts the timestamps and multiplies by 24
Uses TEXT with yyyy-mm or pivot grouping
